title: Master Class | Caro-Kann | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Black answers the king's-pawn with the pawn to c6 — the Caro-Kann.
We grab the centre with the pawn to d4.

Black contests it with d5, attacking our e4-pawn — so we must deal with that. Options include the knight to c3, the pawn to e5 for the Advance, capturing on d5, or the line that flies under the radar.
The pawn to f3 — the Fantasy Variation. It defends the e4-pawn and preserves our big pawn centre.
Black captures on e4 — not a mistake, but it has to be followed up correctly.
We recapture on e4 — a pawn trade leaving us two pawns in the centre.

Black follows up correctly with the pawn to e5. It looks like we can just take, but never forget development in the opening: after taking on e5, the queen to h4 is a fork — check on the king while hitting the e4-pawn at the same time.
So we prevent the queen coming to h4 not by pushing a pawn but by developing — the knight to f3.
Black develops the bishop to g4. Taking on e5 is still bad — not for a check, but because it allows a queen trade that drags our king into the centre.
The bishop to c4 — the most active square, aiming straight at f7, the weakest square on the board.
Black plays the knight to d7. A very sharp opening — we have sacrifices ready on f7.
We castle, continuing development. Notice both the c4-bishop and the f1-rook aim at f7 — only our own knight is in the way, and it's easy to move, after which f7 comes under heavy fire.
Black plays the bishop to d6 — a mistake, because it fails to defend f7, which is guarded only by the king, and the king is a poor defender.

The bishop takes f7 with check — a sacrifice, giving a bishop for a pawn to crack open the king. If the king recaptures, moving the knight is a discovered check that wins the bishop back; the best try is the king to e7, though Black is still losing.

Black plays the king to f8 — the umbrella method, hiding behind our bishop. We can't win with a discovered check yet, so we step back and retreat the bishop — but with a distracting move that forces a reaction.
The bishop to e6 — sacrificing again: if Black takes it, his king lands directly in the rook's line of fire. He can defend by capturing the knight, but he's still in big trouble.
Black plays the knight to f6, covering the rook — but forgetting the g4-bishop.
We take on g4, winning a piece — and if Black recaptures, he exposes himself to a discovered check again.
Black recaptures with the knight on g4. Now notice the king and queen sit a knight's move apart — so picture a knight landing on the square that forks them and wins the queen.
The knight to g5 with check — the fast route to that fork. If the king moves, it loses the knight and mate follows.
Black covers the check with the knight to f6.
The knight to e6 with check — the fork, winning the queen, and the game is basically over.
Black plays the king to e7. Losing the queen for nothing ends the game.
We take the queen, and after the recapture we're up a full queen for a piece. Now just complete development — but first make sure the d4-pawn is well protected.
The pawn to c3, supporting d4 with a pawn chain to keep the centre intact.
Black contests the file with the rook. Our centre is safe — now we complete development, since the bishop and knight are still on their home squares.
The bishop to g5 — developing with a pin on the f6-knight. A pin means the knight can't move without exposing its king. Next we'll develop the knight to d2 and maybe c4.

Black plays the pawn to h6. When you're up material, a good rule is to trade pieces — like taking a deal to remove ten players from each side when the opponent is already a man down: one against zero is easy.
So we trade the bishop for the knight, following the trade-when-ahead principle.
Black recaptures with the knight on f6.
The knight to d2 — developing the last piece and protecting the pawn so his knight can't take it.
Black plays the pawn to g5 — which doesn't do much, but it creates a weak square: one that can no longer be defended by pawns. The f5-square is now weak.
The rook to f5 — occupying that outpost, a piece planted on a weak square, and attacking the e5-pawn to bait a capture on d4.
We could also have manoeuvred a knight to that outpost.
A manoeuvre is just a sequence of moves with one piece.
The knight route from c4 to e3 to f5 was possible, but the rook is faster.
Black takes the pawn — and always look for a better move than the obvious recapture.
The pawn to e5. The bishop and knight sit one square apart, unforkable by a knight — but a pawn can fork: e5 attacks both, and crucially the rook defends the e5-pawn so the bishop can't take it.
Black takes our pawn on c3 — and again, don't just recapture.
The pawn takes the bishop on d6 with check first — recapturing on c3 instead would allow the bishop to c5 with check, and the fork would evaporate.
Black must answer the check with the king. Notice the queen x-rays the king — so the knight can leave with a double check.
The knight to e4 with a double check — knight and queen checking at once. Double checks can't be blocked; the king has to move.
Black's king goes to c7. Now we ensnare the king or win a pile of material.
The queen to d6 with check — an in-between move bringing another piece in. He can't take, since the queen is protected by the knight; the king moves back, and then we take the knight.
Black plays the king to b6 — and it's basically over, up a queen and a knight with a mating attack.
We take the free knight on f6, then go for the mate.
Black grabs on b2 — but it's mate in two.
The knight to d7 with check.
Black's king to a6 — and the finishing move is the hard one to see.
The queen to a3 — checkmate: the rook cuts off the king's escape, the knight covers a square, and the queen delivers the check.
The knight to d5 would not have been mate in two.
Because the knight would block the rook's line.
It would cut the rook's axis to b5, giving the king a flight square.
The king to b5 would escape.
A clean game, showing the fork, the pin, the discovered and double checks, and the mating net.
